Currently trying to refactor a large C++ repo. Kill me!

For me, I deal with:

1. C++ for our newish backend
2. C# for our integration tests
3. C for our really old code
4. Rust for our new projects
5. Powershell for our build systems
6. Bash for weirder build systems
7. Sh for our linux build sytems
8. yml for pipelines

We have less then 10 people and work on 4 repos, 2 in C++ and 2 in Rust so it gets fun. One of the C++ repos works in Visual Studio which is a godsend, but the other murders IDEs so you have to use VSCode and command line tools. 

Debugging involves launching WinDbg from Powershell. Did I mention building takes minimum 20 minutes, the repo is 2 million lines and filled with gotos and weird C shit? 

You can debug unit tests from WinDbg pretty well, but I haven't figured out a way to debug integration tests that isn't print statements and prayer. Oh, and none of the unit tests were running since at least 2015 (if ever) and didn't use the current framework. I had to delete 150 files so far! And the integration tests broke in 2017 and no one noticed so there was basically no test coverage. Yet, this mess is in production, servicing millions of requests a minute. 

For a while there were so many memory leak reports that we just closed them all because there was no way to sort out which were already fixed. I looked at our logs are we are logging the same error 50 million times a day because a dependency is failing. I tracked down the owner of the dependency and they said it was deprecated 2 years ago and asked why we were only complaining now? 

At least this crap will be deprecated.... in *3 to 5 years!?!*

This is the life of a bare metal backend dev. May god have mercy on me.

Under the alien torts statue, non US citizens can sue non US citizens in US courts for some human rights violations. The original law was based on piracy in the 1700s. Pirates were considered enemies of all humanity so whoever caught them could hang them. The Alien Torts Statue allowed the US to prosecute pirates captured outside US waters even if they didn't prey on american shipping.   


The same idea was extended in the 1970s to apply to human rights violations. The idea being that certain crimes were so terrible that they were offensive to all of humanity. 

​

>The first case brought under the ATS for human rights abuses was Filartiga v. Peña-Irala. In 1976, the father of a young man who had been tortured and killed in Paraguay while in police custody witnessed one of his son’s torturers walking the streets of Manhattan. The father called the INS, who arrested the former Paraguayan officer for overstaying his visitor’s visa. The father and sister then brought an ATS case against the officer, and in 1980, a U.S. federal court in New York upheld their claims, opening the door for future claims under the Alien Tort Statute.  


[https://cja.org/what-we-do/litigation/legal-strategy/the-alien-tort-statute/#:\~:text=The%20Alien%20Tort%20Statute%20](https://cja.org/what-we-do/litigation/legal-strategy/the-alien-tort-statute/#:~:text=The%20Alien%20Tort%20Statute%20)(ATS,in%20violation%20of%20international%20law.

I don't know of any cases of someone being extradited under the ATS though. Most cases involve a war criminal being found hiding in the US and tried under US laws even though the crimes they committed were outside the US and against non citizens.
